evaluation.positioning_hook: A timid death-tally clerk with erased powers is forced into a monster-hunting squad, and discovers his panic may be the only thing standing between his office and annihilation.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible: a reluctant office drone with hidden powers gets dragged into a supernatural action mission. The comedy-forward team dynamic broadens the appeal, though the very specific world and slang will skew it toward genre buyers rather than four-quadrant audiences.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast in the opening pages: Francis wakes from a nightmare, returns to a cubicle counting death tolls, then gets conscripted because his wrist device reads him as a SINON. The mission structure and the 'what does he do?' mystery are clear and easy to pitch.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Francis has a clean underdog engine — anxious, funny, and secretly dangerous — and the squad is built from strong comic contrasts. The supporting players are vivid enough to pop, but the page is still more about their banter than deep personal contradiction.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The retro-futurist office setting, death-toll bureaucracy, and anomalous power system give the script a distinct angle. It still plays in familiar monster-team territory, but the corporate absurdity and multilingual banter make it feel authored.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Once Doreen recruits Francis, the script moves with real forward drive into the London fight and the escalating reveal of his power. The main drag is that the setup spends a fair amount of time on character introductions before the mission engine fully ignites.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea — a powerless-seeming office worker whose outbursts can erase reality — is fresh and instantly understandable. The execution is still mostly a first-pass introduction, but the combination of cubicle drudgery and cosmic threat has a strong 'why this works' quality.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Comirum feels like a lived-in institution with its own hierarchy, slang, and internal logic, from the death-toll board to the wrist device to the SINON designation. The world is specific enough to generate story, though this excerpt is still mostly showing the surface rules.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a clear irreverent register: bureaucratic fantasy, gross-out jokes, multilingual insults, and sudden violence all sit in the same lane. The tone is distinctive enough that a buyer can picture the movie in one sentence.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Francis' erased-memory flashes and the mystery around what a SINON really is suggest more beneath the surface. Right now, though, the script is still prioritizing setup and comic momentum over deeper emotional excavation.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Francis/Ploy/Clara/Hal/Toast/Doreen mix creates a usable ensemble engine, with each character generating a different comic and tactical function. The relationships are lively, but the excerpt hasn't yet turned them into a truly interdependent dramatic system.

lead_characters.name: Francis Booker
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s to early 30s, office worker with anomalous powers, likely working-class-coded outsider.
lead_characters.hook: Francis is a terrified logistics clerk at Comirum who would rather count death tolls than enter the field, but his body keeps hinting at a power he doesn't understand. He reads as anxious, funny, and self-protective, with a buried capacity that only surfaces when he's cornered; the nightmare flashes and nosebleeds suggest a bigger identity crisis under the deadpan office routine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network — fast, defensive, and funny under pressure — with the added payoff of a late-blooming power reveal that lets the actor pivot from comic panic to genuine spectacle.

lead_characters.name: Doreen
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 40s-50s, authority figure, corporate/military-adjacent leadership presence.
lead_characters.hook: Doreen is the hard-edged boss who knows exactly how the machine works and has no patience for Francis' resistance. She carries the authority of someone who has already made peace with ugly institutional choices, and the script gives her just enough dry humor to feel dangerous rather than generic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Viola Davis in Fences or Jodie Foster in The Mauritanian their command-room authority — a controlled, high-status performance where every line lands as policy, threat, or reluctant care.

lead_characters.name: Hal
lead_characters.hook: Hal is the loud, swaggering frontline fighter who treats combat like a barroom story and humiliation like a hobby. He is funny because he is so sure of himself, but the script also lets him read as a real operator, which keeps him from becoming pure comic relief.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Dave Bautista in Guardians of the Galaxy — a physically dominant role that still needs timing, vanity, and a surprising amount of warmth.

lead_characters.name: Clara
lead_characters.hook: Clara is a coke-fueled chaos engine with a knife in one hand and a flirtation in the other. She is written as volatile, funny, and dangerous, with enough self-awareness to keep her from collapsing into stereotype, and she gives the team its most unpredictable energy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that made Margot Robbie in Birds of Prey or Jennifer Lawrence in The Hunger Games feel electric — a feral, charismatic performance that gets to be sexy, reckless, and lethal in the same breath.

lead_characters.name: Toast
lead_characters.demographics: Non-human robot, adult-coded intelligence, male-presenting voice/performance.
lead_characters.hook: Toast is the deadpan robotic tactician who speaks like a superior algorithm and treats everyone else like a statistical inconvenience. The joke is his contempt, but the function is precision: he gives the squad its cold logic and its driest comic counterpoint.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of voice/performance showcase that gave Alan Tudyk in Rogue One or Bradley Cooper as Rocket the chance to build a character entirely through timing, attitude, and vocal control.

lead_characters.name: Ploy
lead_characters.hook: Ploy is the loud, flirtatious, bass-obsessed teammate who moves like she has already decided the room belongs to her. She bridges the script's multilingual texture and its action-comedy rhythm, and she is the first one to clock Francis as more than he admits.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of breakout-supporting role that gave Awkwafina in Ocean's 8 or Karen Fukuhara in The Boys a chance to be funny, physical, and instantly memorable without carrying the whole movie.

lead_characters.name: Jerry
lead_characters.demographics: Male, adult, cyborg wolf-man, comic supporting player.
lead_characters.hook: Jerry is the friendly, hungry, physically imposing oddball who turns the office into a surreal workplace ecosystem. He is mostly a comic texture character here, but he helps sell the world as one where the bizarre is normalized.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing creature role that lets an actor lean into prosthetics, physical comedy, and pure personality — the sort of thing that can become a fan favorite off a handful of moments.

casting_characteristics: One lead with a wide emotional range from panic to power
Multilingual dialogue for Ploy and Clara

technical.vfx_details: Multicolor energy blasts, erasure effects, glitch effects, regeneration, and a brief teleport/light transport effect.
technical.sfx_needs: Creature makeup/prosthetics for the wolf-man and zombie British antagonist, practical weapon gags, blood effects, and breakaway glass.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: genre-forward theatrical or streamer original with action-comedy positioning.

budget.note: The office material is contained, but the London night fight, creature work, energy effects, and regeneration/glitch visuals push this beyond a simple indie containment play.

casting.note: Francis needs a lead who can play panic, deadpan comedy, and late-breaking power without losing sympathy, while Toast, Jerry, and Clara each require highly specific performance textures.

development.note: The opening establishes a strong world and team, but the script is still carrying a lot of setup before the central Francis power reveal fully pays off in action.

comp_set.title: Deadpool
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the self-aware profanity, comic violence, and antihero-forward genre playfulness.

comp_set.why_it_comps: The ensemble banter, oddball species mix, and outsider-hero dynamic echo the same crowd-pleasing team chemistry.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre audiences who like irreverent action-comedy with a strong ensemble and a reluctant underdog lead.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44, slightly male-skewing but playable to women through the ensemble humor and character chemistry; strongest with streaming-native genre viewers.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary setting keeps the base manageable, but the creature effects, night exteriors, action coverage, and VFX-powered power reveal push it into mid-budget genre territory.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals execs building genre-comedy slates
mid-budget action producers looking for a franchiseable lead
boutique genre financiers with a taste for ensemble IP
director-driven buyers seeking a breakout visual-comedy feature
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where comic-book energy, workplace satire, and creature-action can coexist without needing tentpole scale. The script's biggest asset is that it offers a clear tonal promise and a castable ensemble around one anxious lead.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: Francis' arc and the Comirum mission read as a self-contained first outing, and no supporting character is yet defined deeply enough to anchor a separate spin-off.

strengths.what_it_means: That contrast gives the movie a clean commercial identity: a workplace comedy engine that can pivot into action without losing its hook. Buyers looking for a genre concept they can explain in one breath will respond to the cubicle-to-combat escalation.
strengths.evidence: The opening death-toll spreadsheet, the comic-sans board, and Francis being dragged from logistics into a London kill mission.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Francis is a strong reluctant-hero lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The role has a built-in arc from panic to competence, which is exactly the kind of part that can launch or reframe a young actor. Casting teams will see a playable mix of comedy, vulnerability, and late-breaking spectacle.
strengths.evidence: He repeatedly insists he cannot do the mission, then ultimately triggers the beam that erases the zombie.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble has real comic chemistry.
strengths.what_it_means: The team is differentiated enough that scenes can generate energy from personality alone, which is valuable for both trailers and audience word-of-mouth. That makes the project more than a single-gimmick premise.
strengths.evidence: Hal's swagger, Clara's chaos, Toast's contempt, Ploy's bass-heavy confidence, and Doreen's deadpan authority all collide cleanly in the briefing and fight.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world has a usable internal mythology.
strengths.what_it_means: Comirum, SINONs, the wrist meter, and the death-toll bureaucracy create a repeatable system that can support sequenced missions and a recognizable brand identity. That gives the script more commercial shape than a one-off monster romp.
strengths.evidence: The wrist device measuring outbursts, the SINON designation, and the logistics division's death-toll board.

strengths.what_it_means: The script knows how to mix profanity, absurdity, and action without losing its comic register, which helps it stand out in a crowded genre field. That tonal clarity is attractive to buyers who want something that feels marketable from page one.
strengths.evidence: The comic-sans death board, the British zombie's tea banter, and Clara's gunfire one-liners all live in the same lane.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, marketable genre package: a reluctant office clerk with hidden reality-warping powers, a vivid misfit squad, and a contained-enough world to sell as a mid-budget streaming or theatrical action-comedy. The concept is easy to pitch, the ensemble is castable, and the script already has the kind of tonal identity that can separate it from generic monster-team material.

items.area: The opening spends a long time on setup before the mission engine locks in.
items.detail: The nightmare, office routine, donut banter, and team introductions all work as texture, but they delay the moment when the central premise becomes a true forward-driving engine. For a feature, that means the first act is carrying a lot of explanatory weight before the audience gets the full promise of the concept.

items.area: Francis' power rules are still mostly mystery language.
items.detail: The script tells us his outbursts are anomalous and that he can 'do anything,' but the trigger logic and limits are still vague through the climax. That keeps the reveal fun, but it also makes the power system feel more like a punchline than a fully bankable mechanic.

items.area: The ensemble is vivid, but the emotional stakes are light.
items.detail: Hal, Clara, Toast, Ploy, and Doreen all pop on the page, yet the excerpt mostly uses them for banter and tactical function rather than deeper relational pressure. A buyer will see the chemistry, but also notice that the dramatic engine is still more comic than emotionally loaded.

items.area: The London fight leans on moderate VFX and creature work.
items.detail: The regenerating zombie, erasure beam, glitch effects, and transport-light moments all add up to a real effects package, even before the practical creature makeup and blood work. That keeps the project out of microbudget territory and makes the budget conversation more sensitive than the office setting alone suggests.

issues.headline: The script's biggest buyer conversation is timing: the premise is clear, but the first act spends a fair amount of pages getting to the actual engine. Beyond that, the movie is commercially legible, but the power-system mystery and effects package will be the main questions around how confidently it can be mounted.
